strengths: The subject matter itself that this paper deals with is of great scientific importance beyond the toy example.

The presentation of this paper is very excellent. It is well thought out for a diverse audience, especially since it provides sufficient background knowledge and motivation for the research questions, even for the acoustic communication systems of whales, for which many machine learning researchers may not have domain knowledge.

The methods proposed to gain insight into the causal structure of the target of interest from the latent variable space extracted by machine learning data analysis are very appealing, a new approach to cross‑disciplinary thinking inspired by pharmacology dose‑response.
Surprising findings, in Figure 1: “The 9R type was never part of the training data, yet our network learns to generate codas that resemble this type (Sec. 4).”
Overall, this is a fascinating paper and well‑written paper.

Generally speaking, the notion of using generative models to drive hypothesis formulation and testing for unknown processes may have profound implications for basic science research, and the particular process studied here (whale communication) is refreshingly off the beaten path for ICLR.
The proposed CDEV method is explained clearly and with sufficient information to allow for replication (though the data and model appear to be closed).
The paper introduces an approach for exploring scientific findings from a sperm communication system using deep generative models and causal inference techniques.
weaknesses: What is the advantage of learning a representation (t,x) using a deep generative model in the hope that t will represent some intuitive features (like number of clicks and click regularity), if these very features can be extracted from the raw data algorithmically (as is done in this work, for evaluation)?

The work presents an original application of disentangled representation learning but does not contain novel methodological contributions; the authors essentially trained an existing method and applied fairly standard qualitative evaluation strategies to assess disentanglement.

The authors should clarify what they mean by disentanglement, since their definition (which I inferred from their experiment) seems different from the one I know and which is widely used: typically, disentanglement means the following: every component of the latent representation influences one and only one interpretable factor of variation.

Figure 4 does not correspond to the usual notion of “disentanglement”. Here, all the dimensions of t have an impact on the number of clicks. The interesting thing is that it seems only one dimension of t has a positive impact, while all the others have a negative impact.

Figure 5 still does not correspond to the usual notion of disentanglement, since, again, every dimension of t_i has an impact on the “inter‑click” interval and the “coda regularity”; it is just that one of the bits has a monotonic influence while the others are non‑monotonic.
The experiments did not convince that the fiwGAN algorithm can robustly discover natural factors of variation in the data; there is no evidence of robustness to reinitialization (multiple seeds).
In Figure 4 the curves that go down seem to go up again after t = 10; it is unclear whether they become positive if the range of t is extended further.
The surprising findings in Figure 1 require stronger evidence that the model can generate reasonable samples never seen during training; the presented sample may be cherry‑picked.
The framing in terms of causal inference feels unjustified, since one has full control over both x and t, so there is not a direct causal effect from x to t, making causal inference trivial.
In the introduction the variable t was not defined, making it hard to follow what is meant.
The description of fiwGAN is imprecise; the loss that is optimized should be written down explicitly.
Figure 2 contains an inconsistency: the code t is described as binary, but the rest of the paper assumes t is Rademacher with support {‑1, 1} instead of {0, 1}.
In Section 3 the meaning of “entanglement” is unclear, and the separation between theory/method and experiments is not sufficiently clear.
The proposed CDEV method is applied to a single model trained on a small amount of data from a single unknown process, limiting its interest to the broader ICLR community.
The model uses unconventional assumptions (the specific use of 5 discrete inputs) rooted in a rudimentary understanding of the data process, and the authors provide no justification for this choice.

Domain knowledge appears to be a substantive input to the CDEV algorithm at several levels (choice of discrete inputs, data selection, determining extreme latent values, outcome functions), which may limit the generality of the method.

The authors have not provided sufficient evidence to support their application‑specific claims; it is unclear whether confounders (e.g., water temperature) have been ruled out for the observed mean spectral frequency effects.

It is not demonstrated that the GAN has adequately fit the underlying data distribution, raising the possibility that observed interventional effects are due to model artifacts rather than genuine communication phenomena.
The experiments are insufficient; the authors do not validate that the generated latents correspond to actual latent structures of the data rather than artifacts of the model.
The paper lacks comparisons with existing disentanglement methods using VAEs (e.g., betaVAE).
In figures 4 and 6 it seems that only one bit differs while other bits are generally similar, suggesting limited variation.
The manuscript does not discuss limitations and future research directions for the proposed method.
It is unclear whether the proposed method can be generalized to other animals' communication systems or other fields; the paper would be more solid by including results on another dataset.
